sermon:
## Before the Ask, the Thanksgiving
*How grace softens the ground before it ever makes a request*

**Text:** Philemon 1-7 · **Supporting:** Colossians 4:9 · Romans 5:8 · 2 Corinthians 9:13 · 1 John 3:18

Most of us, when we are about to ask someone for something hard, lead with the ask. We get to the point. We have learned that flattery is manipulation, and we would rather be honest than oily, so we say the difficult thing first and let the chips fall.

Paul does not do that. He has a request coming that will cost Philemon his pride, his property, and his right to be angry. And he spends seven verses before he gets anywhere near it, naming what God has already made true of the man he is about to ask.

That is not technique. That is theology.

**Grace names a man before it asks anything of him**
Paul opens the way he always opens, with grace and the God it comes from. "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (Philemon 3). It reads like a formula until you remember that Paul is writing from a chain. He is "a prisoner of Christ Jesus" (Philemon 1), and the first word out of the prisoner's mouth is grace.

Then he turns to Philemon directly. "I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints" (Philemon 4-5). Hear what Paul is doing. He is not buttering up a man he intends to use. He is telling the truth about what God has done in him. The love is real. The faith is real. Philemon has a track record, and Paul has heard about it.

We tend to think of identity as something we build and grace as something that rescues us after we have failed at building it. Paul thinks the other way around. Before Philemon is a slaveholder with a grievance, he is a man God has already filled with love for the saints. That is the truer thing. The grievance is real, but it is not the deepest fact about him, and Paul is going to make the appeal to the deepest fact.

**The proof of grace is a refreshed heart, not a managed reputation**
Watch the word Paul reaches for. "For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you" (Philemon 7). Refreshed. The word carries the sense of rest given to the weary, the way a man coming in from the field is given water and a place to sit down. Philemon has been the kind of believer whose home in Colossae is a place where tired Christians breathe easier.

This is the evidence Paul trusts. Not Philemon's orthodoxy on paper. Not his standing in the city. The hearts of God's people have actually been rested by this man, and Paul has heard about it from the inside of a prison.

There is a quiet weight here for everyone who has ever wanted to be known as a generous person more than they wanted to be one. Paul is not commending Philemon's reputation for refreshing the saints. He is commending the refreshing itself. The love that John refused to leave abstract, "let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth" (1 John 3:18) — that is the love Paul has heard reports of. It showed up in deeds. It rested actual people.

And Paul prays it would go further. "I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ" (Philemon 6). He wants the faith already in Philemon to work its way all the way out, into the one room where it has not yet been tested.

Because Paul knows the room. There is a man coming home.

**The pattern under the letter is the pattern of the cross**
Here is what we usually miss because we are reading too fast. Paul is doing to Philemon exactly what God did to Paul, and to us.

God did not approach us with the demand first. "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). The kindness came before the obedience. The grace came before the change. We did not clean ourselves up and then receive the love; the love arrived first, and the love is what does the cleaning. Paul learned this on a road to Damascus, knocked flat by a mercy he had spent his life persecuting. He never got over the order of it. Grace first. Always grace first.

So when Paul prepares Philemon for a costly request by first naming the grace already in him, he is not softening a man up. He is preaching the gospel to him in miniature. He is saying: you are not what you are about to be asked to give up. You are a man whose heart has been remade to refresh other hearts. Now there is one more heart to refresh, and it belongs to someone you swore you would never refresh again.

I have done the opposite of this more times than I can count. I have led with the indictment because the indictment felt righteous, and I have called my impatience honesty. I have wanted people to repent before I would be warm to them, which is precisely backward, and which is precisely not how God dealt with me. The grace that found me did not wait for me to deserve the warmth. It went first.

That is the order Paul is establishing here, and it is the order Onesimus is about to walk into. Before he reaches Philemon's door, the ground has been prepared by a man already formed by grace, addressed by grace, prayed for by grace. The hardest letter in Paul's hand begins this gently on purpose.

Grace prepares the ground first.

## No Longer a Slave
*Why Paul, who could command, chooses instead to appeal*

**Text:** Philemon 8-16 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:28 · Colossians 3:11 · 1 Corinthians 7:22 · 2 Corinthians 5:17

Paul has the authority to make this an order. He says so plainly. "Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required" (Philemon 8). He is an apostle. He led Philemon to Christ. He could write four sentences of command and be entirely within his rights.

He refuses.

"Yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you — I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus" (Philemon 9). The man with the authority lays the authority down and asks. And the whole letter turns on why.

**Paul will not command, because the gospel works by remaking, not by forcing**
There is a kind of obedience you can compel, and there is a kind you cannot. You can compel a slaveholder to release a slave. You cannot compel him to receive that slave as a brother. The first is a transaction. The second is a transformation, and transformation does not come at the point of a command.

So Paul appeals. "I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment" (Philemon 10). Notice the language. Father and child. The runaway slave who fled Philemon's house has become Paul's son in the faith, born again inside a Roman jail. The man Philemon owned is now Paul's child, which makes him, in some unbearable new way, family to Philemon too.

Then Paul makes a pun he cannot resist. Onesimus means useful. "Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me" (Philemon 11). The runaway who was worse than worthless — a thief, by the hints in verse 18, and a fugitive — is now genuinely useful, and not as a tool but as a person. The gospel did not just improve Onesimus. It changed what kind of thing he is.

**The gospel does not keep the old categories. It abolishes them.**
This is the hinge of the letter, and we are tempted to read past it because we already believe it in theory. Paul sends Onesimus back, and he sends him back under an entirely new name.

"I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart" (Philemon 12). My very heart. Paul calls a runaway slave his own heart, and tells the man who owns him to handle him accordingly.

Then the verdict that the whole book has been building toward: "For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother — especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord" (Philemon 15-16).

No longer as a bondservant. More than a bondservant. A beloved brother.

This is the same Paul who wrote, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). It is the same Paul who told the Colossians — Philemon's own congregation — "Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all" (Colossians 3:11). Paul is not writing abstractly in those letters. He has a specific slave and a specific master in mind. The doctrine has a name and an address, and the address is Philemon's house.

Understand what Paul is asking. He is not asking Philemon to be a kinder master. He is asking him to stop being a master at all in the only sense that finally matters, to look at the man he owned and see a brother who will sit beside him at the Lord's table for eternity. "For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:22). The legal status has not changed on paper. The real status has changed completely. And Paul is asking Philemon to let the real status overrun the legal one.

**We keep the old names because the old names protect our right to be angry**
Here is where this stops being ancient history. We do this. I do this.

We have categories for the people who have wronged us, and we hold onto them with both hands. The one who betrayed me. The one who took what was mine. The one who walked out. We keep them filed under the offense, because the file is what justifies the distance, and the distance feels like safety. As long as a person stays in the category of "what they did to me," I never have to receive them. The category does the work of keeping them out.

The gospel comes after the category. It says: that man is no longer a thief; he is a brother. That woman is no longer the one who betrayed you; she is a daughter of God bought at the same price you were. "Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17). And if the new has come for him, then your old name for him is a lie, however true it once was.

This is Christ's doing, and we should not soften it. The reason Onesimus comes home as a brother and not a slave is that both men have been bought by the same blood. The Lord who freed Onesimus is the Lord who owns Philemon. They share a Master now, and you cannot share a Master and keep calling each other property. The cross flattens the floor. It puts the slaveholder and the slave on their knees at the same height, and from that height neither one can look down on the other again.

Paul will not command this, because a commanded reception is not reception. He appeals — and the appeal is the gospel asking a free man to do freely what only grace could make him willing to do.

Receive him as a brother.

## Charge It to My Account
*The man who steps into the gap and pays a debt he never owed*

**Text:** Philemon 17-25 · **Supporting:** 2 Corinthians 5:21 · Isaiah 53:6 · Colossians 2:14 · Romans 8:32

There is a moment in this letter where Paul stops appealing and starts paying. He has named Philemon's love. He has reframed Onesimus from slave to brother. But there is still a debt sitting between the two men, real money and real theft, and no amount of warm language makes a debt disappear. Someone has to deal with it.

So Paul deals with it. He puts his own name on it.

**Receive him as you would receive me**
"So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me" (Philemon 17). Stop on that. Paul does not say, receive him because he has changed, though he has. He does not say, receive him because he is sorry, though he surely is. He says, receive him as you would receive me. Welcome the runaway thief the way you would welcome the apostle who led you to Christ.

That is an extraordinary thing to ask, and Paul knows it, so he immediately makes it possible by absorbing the cost himself. "If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account" (Philemon 18). Charge it to me. Put it on my ledger. Whatever Onesimus took, whatever he owes, send the bill to Paul.

Then, so there is no mistaking it, Paul writes a line in his own hand, the way a man signs a promissory note. "I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it — to say nothing of your owing me even your own self" (Philemon 19). There it is in writing. A signed pledge. Paul will cover the theft of a slave he met in a prison, out of his own pocket, because that is what it costs to put two estranged men back in the same room.

**The debt is not erased. It is moved.**
We need to be precise here, because cheap grace gets this wrong. Paul does not tell Philemon to forget about it. He does not say the debt was small, or that Onesimus did not really mean it, or that we should all just move on. The wrong is named — "if he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything" — and the wrong is real.

The gospel never pretends the debt is not there. It moves the debt.

That is the whole mechanism. Onesimus owes a debt he cannot pay. Philemon holds a debt he has every right to collect. And Paul steps into the space between them, takes the debt off the guilty man, and writes it onto himself. The offender goes free not because the debt vanished but because someone with a clean ledger agreed to carry it on his own account.

If that sounds familiar, it should. This is the shape of the cross, drawn small enough to fit in a personal letter.

"For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is the same accounting. Our debt, charged to his account. His righteousness, credited to ours. "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). Laid on him. The iniquity did not evaporate. It was placed, deliberately, on the one willing to bear it. "He set this aside, nailing it to the cross" (Colossians 2:14) — the very record of debt that stood against us, taken out of the way by being nailed to a body that was not the debtor's.

Charge it to my account is not a clever phrase. It is the gospel in four words. Christ does not look at the debt we owe and call it nothing. He looks at it, names it in full, and tells the Father to put it on his account. Then he signs it with his own hand, and the hand has a nail through it.

**The confidence is in the one who pays, not the one who owes**
Watch how the letter ends, because it ends in confidence, and the confidence is strange. "Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say" (Philemon 21). Even more than I say. Paul does not just expect Philemon to settle the account. He expects him to overshoot it, to do more than reconciliation requires.

Where does that confidence come from? Not from Onesimus, who has nothing to offer but his need. It comes from the one standing in the gap. Paul is sure the reconciliation will hold because Paul himself has guaranteed it with his own name and his own purse. The confidence rests on the payer, never on the debtor.

That is exactly where my assurance has to live, and exactly where I keep trying to move it. I want my standing with God to rest on my account, on my repayment, on my track record finally getting respectable. It never does. The ledger never comes clean by my hand. And the gospel keeps gently taking my eyes off my account and putting them on his. "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" (Romans 8:32). The confidence is in the One who paid, and he has already done even more than I asked.

Paul closes the way he opened, with grace. "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit" (Philemon 25). The letter that began with grace ends with grace, and in between, a man with a clean ledger picked up a debt that was not his, so that a guilty man could come home as if he owed nothing.

That is not a story about Philemon and Onesimus. It is a story about you, and the one who signed your debt in his own blood.

Put the debt on me.
